name: Critical safety incident reporting
short: Tell the state within 15 days when something goes seriously wrong. 24 hours if it is imminent.
trigger: Frontier developers (models above 10^26 FLOP).
protects: Lets the government spot dangerous failures early, like a stolen model or AI helping with an attack.
risk_why: Reports come after something has gone wrong, so they mostly help regulators respond and learn. They rarely prevent the first disaster.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up essentially nothing behind where it would be. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: None worth naming. The only cost is a lawyer's afternoon.
requires: Report a critical safety incident to the state within 15 days of discovering it (California SB 53). | Report within 24 hours if the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. | EU Code of Practice signatories report serious incidents on a 2, 5, 10 or 15 day clock depending on severity. | SB 1047 would have required 72 hours.
baseline: OpenAI and Anthropic already have incident processes under their own frameworks, and both are now legally bound by SB 53 in California. Nothing in the requirement touches training, internal use or release.
reasoning:
There is no pre-release gate in this scope. Incremental reporting hours compete with research only to the extent that specialized staff or extra hiring fail to absorb them. The result is economically negligible on this metric; rounding does not imply that reporting requires literally no work.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is essentially nothing behind its baseline path and China's is essentially nothing behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, essentially nothing, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: A reporting regime creates a record that regulators and plaintiffs can use later, which could make labs more cautious about internal deployments of capable models. That caution, not the filing, is where a cost would come from. We see no evidence of it so far and it would be a cost of liability exposure rather than of the reporting rule itself.
sources: California Bus. & Prof. Code § 22757.13 (SB 53): critical safety incident reporting <https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22757.13> | SB 1047 enrolled text, § 22603(g): 72-hour reporting <https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB1047> | EU GPAI Code of Practice, Safety and Security chapter <https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/118119>

name: Published frontier safety framework
short: Write down how you assess and mitigate catastrophic risk, publish it, and follow it.
trigger: Large frontier developers (revenue above $500M).
protects: Makes each lab commit in public to what it will do if a model turns out to be dangerous.
risk_why: Labs already publish these. Making them binding helps a little by making it harder to quietly drop commitments under pressure.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: Whether being legally bound to your own framework makes a lab write a weaker one or hold a launch to comply with it.
requires: Publish a frontier AI framework covering capability thresholds, mitigations, pre-deployment review, third-party assessment, weight security and incident response (SB 53 § 22757.12). | Review it at least yearly; publish material changes within 30 days with a justification. | Do not make materially false statements about compliance with it. | EU signatories must adopt an equivalent Safety and Security Framework.
baseline: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy is on version 3.4. OpenAI's Preparedness Framework is on version 2, with a companion Frontier Governance Framework written to map onto SB 53 and the EU Code. Google DeepMind and xAI publish frontier safety frameworks. The requirement codifies what every covered lab already publishes.
reasoning:
The estimate concerns legal adherence to a framework beyond voluntary practice. A public hold mostly affects foreign access. Internal holds matter through foregone productivity of the newest model; an already-trained model is not erased from the technical frontier.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: Anthropic's RSP v3.0 explicitly moved away from hard pre-deployment gates toward public goals it grades itself against. A law that makes a framework binding removes that flexibility. If a lab's own threshold is crossed at an awkward moment, a binding framework could force a delay the voluntary version would not. The cost is real but it is the cost of a threshold, and it is priced under the evaluation and safety-case items.
sources: California Bus. & Prof. Code § 22757.12 (SB 53): frontier AI framework <https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22757.12> | Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy, version history <https://www.anthropic.com/rsp-updates> | OpenAI Preparedness Framework v2 <https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/18a02b5d-6b67-4cec-ab64-68cdfbddebcd/preparedness-framework-v2.pdf> | OpenAI Frontier Governance Framework <https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/e37d949b-8c9f-4d76-b99e-4272f4631a7e/openai-frontier-governance-framework.pdf> | GovAI on Anthropic's RSP v3.0 <https://www.governance.ai/analysis/anthropics-rsp-v3-0-how-it-works-whats-changed-and-some-reflections>

name: Transparency report at launch
short: Publish a system card with risk assessment results before or when you deploy.
trigger: All frontier developers; extra content for large ones.
protects: Tells the public what a new model can do and what the lab tested before it shipped.
risk_why: Disclosure alone changes little, but it gives outsiders what they need to catch problems.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up essentially nothing behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: Whether a legally required document ever finishes later than the launch it accompanies.
requires: Before or concurrently with deploying a new frontier model, publish a report with intended uses, restrictions, modalities and, for large developers, summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments and the role of third-party evaluators (SB 53 § 22757.12(c)). | Send the state a summary of internal-use catastrophic-risk assessments every three months. | EU Code signatories file a Model Report at deployment.
baseline: OpenAI publishes a system card with every frontier release (GPT-5.5 on April 23, 2026; GPT-6 Astra on September 3, 2026). Anthropic publishes system cards at launch and Risk Reports every three to six months. The legal document is the system card with a checklist.
reasoning:
A late document can defer public launch without delaying technical development. The small modeled widening comes from less access to U.S. teachers, offset by incremental compliance labor. Its sign is sensitive to the marginal teacher-dependence assumption.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is essentially nothing behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: The definition of deployment is broad. GovAI found that in the first five months of 2026, the frontier models withheld from general release were instead given to select entities under trusted-access programs. If a transparency report is required before any third party touches the model, those programs would have to wait for the write-up. That could cost a week or two on the access clock per model, and it is why the high end of the range is a week.

name: Whistleblower protections
short: Employees can report catastrophic-risk concerns to regulators without retaliation. Complimentary.
trigger: Frontier developers.
protects: Lets employees warn regulators about hidden dangers without being fired or sued.
risk_why: Insiders are often the first to see problems, and several past warnings about lab safety came from employees. Protecting them is one of the cheaper safeguards.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: None. This item is on the menu to make a point about what regulation mostly consists of.
requires: No policy or contract that prevents an employee from reporting a catastrophic-risk danger or a legal violation to the Attorney General, federal authorities or a supervisor (California Labor Code § 1107.1). | Large developers provide an anonymous internal reporting channel with monthly status updates to the reporter. | Post a notice of rights.
baseline: Anthropic and OpenAI both publicly dropped non-disparagement clauses that could have chilled safety disclosures, and both describe internal reporting channels in their frameworks. The law makes that permanent.
reasoning:
Extra investigations are modeled as rare, localized interruptions of research. Benefits from better information, retention or avoided misconduct are not empirically quantified here. A near-zero result should not be interpreted as a judgment on those benefits.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: There is no serious case for a lead cost. The strongest argument against this provision is about litigation risk and morale, not about the race.
sources: California Labor Code § 1107.1 (SB 53) <https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1107.1>

name: Full shutdown capability
short: Be able to turn the model off. The kill switch.
trigger: Covered frontier models (SB 1047 definition); under study for California by executive order.
protects: Makes sure a lab can actually stop a model that goes wrong.
risk_why: A kill switch helps only if someone notices the problem in time and the model hasn't already spread, so the effect is modest.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: Whether a regulator's definition of shutdown ever exceeds what labs already engineer for their own operations.
requires: Implement the capability to promptly enact a full shutdown of training, model operation and derivatives under the developer's control (SB 1047 § 22603(a)). | California's September 2026 executive order asks an expert panel to recommend how a kill switch for frontier models should work.
baseline: Every lab can stop a training run and pull a model from its API. The ability to do so is operational hygiene, not a new engineering program. Anthropic's RSP and OpenAI's frameworks both contemplate pausing deployment as a mitigation.
reasoning:
This prices the frozen developer-controlled shutdown requirement. Engineering changes are one-time, with only the affected research fraction charged. A rule demanding control over every downstream copy would be a different intervention.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: A shutdown requirement that extends to model derivatives held by third parties, or to open-weight models, is not technically achievable and could push a lab to withhold open weights. That would affect China's access more than the U.S. frontier, which would push the price negative rather than positive.
sources: SB 1047 enrolled text, § 22603(a)(2): full shutdown <https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB1047> | California Executive Order N-9-26 on independent oversight and a kill switch <https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/18/governor-newsom-issues-executive-order-to-accelerate-independent-oversight-and-advance-the-creation-of-an-ai-kill-switch/>

name: Annual independent compliance audit
short: An outside auditor checks once a year that you did what your framework says.
trigger: Covered frontier developers (SB 1047 would have started this in 2026).
protects: Checks that labs actually follow their own safety promises.
risk_why: Audits look back at whether labs kept their promises. That keeps promises honest but catches few dangers directly.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: Whether audit findings ever require remediation before a launch.
requires: Retain an independent third-party auditor annually to assess compliance with the safety framework, identify gaps and recommend corrections (SB 1047 § 22603(e)). | Publish a redacted audit report and send it to the Attorney General. | California's 2026 laws SB 813 and AB 1405 set up a framework and registry for independent verification organizations.
baseline: Labs already commission external security audits and, increasingly, external reviews of their safety frameworks. Anthropic commits to seeking public external review of its Risk Reports.
reasoning:
Annual audit findings do not delay every launch. The public-model stream uses a cycle-average approximation; dated checks in the supplied helper verify that an expired hold does not keep delaying later releases.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: An auditor who has to sign off on a framework may demand conservative interpretations of thresholds, which ratchets a lab's own gates tighter. Over several generations that ratchet could add up. It is a second-order effect and we have no data on it.

name: Mandatory internal capability evaluations
short: Run dangerous-capability evaluations on every frontier model before you deploy it.
trigger: Frontier models before external deployment.
protects: Catches dangerous abilities, like helping build weapons, before a model is released.
risk_why: Testing is the main way labs find dangerous abilities. Labs already test, so a mandate mostly locks in and standardizes the practice.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: How much of the evaluation must wait for the final checkpoint rather than a proxy.
requires: Before deployment, run a defined suite of evaluations for chemical, biological, cyber and autonomy capabilities and document the results. | Compare results against published thresholds and record the deployment decision.
baseline: OpenAI's Preparedness Framework says every covered model undergoes its suite of scalable evaluations prior to deployment. Anthropic runs capability assessments under its RSP. GPT-5.5 went through targeted red-teaming for cyber and biology before release. The requirement is already the norm.
reasoning:
Published testing durations anchor possible workloads; only mandatory work beyond the voluntary suite is incremental. Most testing overlaps training, launch preparation and other safety work. Findings requiring new remediation belong to the separate triggered-remediation mechanism.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: Evaluation suites grow. A mandate with a fixed list could add human uplift studies or agentic evaluations that take weeks and cannot run on proxies. And a legal duty to evaluate is a legal duty to act on the result, which turns a measurement into a gate. That gate is priced separately, but a critic would say the two cannot be separated in practice.
sources: AISI, Early lessons from evaluating frontier AI systems <https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/early-lessons-from-evaluating-frontier-ai-systems> | OpenAI Preparedness Framework v2 <https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/18a02b5d-6b67-4cec-ab64-68cdfbddebcd/preparedness-framework-v2.pdf> | GPT-5.5 System Card <https://openai.com/index/gpt-5-5-system-card/>

name: Independent pre-deployment evaluation
short: An approved outside evaluator tests the model and reports before public release.
trigger: Frontier models before external deployment.
protects: Gets independent experts to check for dangerous abilities the lab might miss or play down.
risk_why: Outside testers catch things labs miss or play down, and a launch deadline can't overrule them.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: Whether labs would share checkpoints earlier or simply wait longer at the end.
requires: Give an independent evaluator (a government institute or an approved organization) access to a representative checkpoint before release. | Receive the evaluator's report before public deployment; the report can be redacted for publication. | No fixed access period is set; the evaluator gets what it gets.
baseline: Every major U.S. release now goes through some external testing. UK AISI and U.S. CAISI tested GPT-5.5. METR had ten business days on Claude Opus 5.5 and three weeks on o3 and GPT-5. But access is uneven: Apollo had three days on GPT-6 Astra and SecureBio six calendar days. The practice exists; the mandate makes it universal and makes the report a precondition.
reasoning:
Qualifying evaluations already conducted voluntarily are reused. External evaluator service, queueing, existing access runway and final-report tails are distinct. This is not a claim that every observed evaluation caused its entire elapsed duration as delay.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: Evaluators are capacity-constrained. If every frontier release from four labs must queue for the same institute, the queue is the delay, and it lands in the lab's release schedule whether or not the model is done. METR itself says deployment-tied evaluations often leave little time for thorough analysis. A mandate that fixes that problem by adding time is, by construction, adding time. And the labs' own behavior suggests they treat evaluator windows as release-blocking rather than parallel.
sources: GPT-5.5 System Card: external evaluations <https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-5-5> | GPT-6 Astra deployment safety page <https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra> | METR evaluation of Claude Opus 5.5 <https://metr.org/blog/2026-09-22-claude-opus-5-5/> | METR evaluation of o3 and o4-mini <https://metr.org/evaluations/openai-o3-report/> | METR Frontier Risk Report, Feb–Mar 2026 <https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-19-frontier-risk-report/> | AISI, Early lessons from evaluating frontier AI systems <https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/early-lessons-from-evaluating-frontier-ai-systems> | Expanding External Access to Frontier AI Models (arXiv 2601.11916) <https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11916>

name: Twenty business days of evaluator access
short: Outside evaluators get at least four weeks with the model before it ships.
trigger: Frontier models before external deployment (the EU Code of Practice's suggested period).
protects: Gives government testers time to find dangers before the public gets a model.
risk_why: Extra time helps only with dangers testers can find in a few weeks, and it doesn't cover the lab's own use of the model.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: Whether labs respond by sharing checkpoints four weeks earlier or by shipping four weeks later.
requires: Provide independent external evaluators with at least 20 business days of access to the model before public release. | The EU Code of Practice describes this as appropriate for most systemic risks and evaluation methods; METR's guidance for lab staff repeats it.
baseline: Actual windows in 2025 and 2026 ran from three days (GPT-6 Astra, Apollo) to three weeks (o3, GPT-5). Ten business days on Claude Opus 5.5 is the recent norm at the generous end. A 20-business-day floor is two to three weeks more than typical practice.
reasoning:
Twenty business days is modeled as a 28-calendar-day convention. Existing access can satisfy much of that requirement. Earlier sharing is allowed; a material checkpoint reset can create an additional residual tail. Holidays and particular legal counting conventions are not separately forecast.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: Four weeks is a real number in a field where METR measures the frontier doubling every 105 days. If commercial availability drives revenue, and revenue drives compute purchases, a systematic four-week delay on every release compounds into a slower frontier. And the internal-versus-public distinction may be thinner than it looks: OpenAI's internal-to-external gap is only a few weeks, so a four-week floor could exceed the lab's own cadence and force it to hold the internal frontier too.

name: Triggered red-team and remediation
short: If an evaluation crosses a danger threshold, do elevated testing and fix it before anyone can use it.
trigger: Any frontier model whose evaluations cross a defined capability threshold.
protects: When a model shows warning signs, outside experts try to break it before release.
risk_why: It targets the riskiest models, but only if the warning signs are noticed.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: How often thresholds get crossed and whether safeguards must be in place for internal use as well as release.
requires: When a pre-deployment evaluation crosses a capability threshold, conduct elevated testing (expert red-teaming, possibly uplift studies). | Implement and verify safeguards before deployment; if the threshold governs internal use, before internal deployment too.
baseline: Both major frameworks already have this shape. OpenAI's Preparedness Framework requires safeguards at High capability; its GPT-6 Astra card says safeguards were required even for internal deployment because of cyber capability. Anthropic's RSP has ASL-3 and ASL-4 safeguards tied to thresholds. Thresholds are now being crossed routinely rather than hypothetically.
reasoning:
The relevant probability is an incremental binding intervention, not merely a model crossing a risk threshold. Prepared mitigations reduce remaining work. Joint incidence and remedy difficulty could be more correlated than the base independent priors.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: Thresholds only get crossed more often from here. If every frontier model now triggers elevated testing, the conditional becomes unconditional and this item becomes a standing four-to-six-week gate. Worse, if regulators rather than labs define the threshold and the remediation standard, the lab loses the ability to prepare safeguards in advance for a threshold it can anticipate. That would move the central price toward a month and push more of it onto the internal clock.
sources: AISI, Early lessons from evaluating frontier AI systems <https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/early-lessons-from-evaluating-frontier-ai-systems> | GPT-6 Astra deployment safety page <https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra> | OpenAI Preparedness Framework v2 <https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/18a02b5d-6b67-4cec-ab64-68cdfbddebcd/preparedness-framework-v2.pdf> | Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy <https://www.anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy>

name: Safety case before deployment
short: Write a structured argument that the model is safe to release, and have it reviewed, before you release it.
trigger: Frontier models before external deployment.
protects: Makes a lab show a model is safe enough before release, instead of critics having to show it isn't.
risk_why: Shifting the burden of proof is a big change: the lab has to argue why the model is safe enough, not just report that tests passed.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China loses about 2 days more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: Nobody has published how long a frontier safety case takes to write or review.
requires: Before external deployment, produce a safety case: a structured argument, with evidence, that the model's risks are below defined levels given its safeguards. | Submit it to a regulator or independent reviewer and receive sign-off before release.
baseline: Anthropic's Risk Reports are the closest published artifact. Under RSP v3.4 they go to external reviewers within a week of the Board, and reviewers are asked to respond within 30 days. OpenAI's Capabilities and Safeguards Reports serve a similar internal role. No lab currently waits for an outside sign-off before launch.
reasoning:
The long-tail approval model can materially defer external availability while having a much smaller effect on technical progress. Internal-use restrictions enter research productivity separately. On a publicly deployable-model metric, this policy would have a substantially larger positive delay.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is about 2 days behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, about 1 day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: We have no data on how long these take. AISI has written about safety cases as a method; no lab has published one for a frontier launch with a timeline. A regulator's review could take far longer than 30 days the first few times, and a lab that fails review restarts the clock. If the practical review tail is six weeks rather than two, this item costs a month and a half of release delay per generation, and if the lab holds internal rollout for the sign-off, it costs the same on the U.S. clock.
sources: Anthropic RSP v3.4: external review of Risk Reports <https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/files/4zrzovbb/website/0bacdc8440ea96e62a8766d99ebe1d4eea6d5f3a.pdf> | AISI, How can safety cases be used to help with frontier AI safety? <https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/how-can-safety-cases-be-used-to-help-with-frontier-ai-safety> | OpenAI Preparedness Framework v2 <https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/18a02b5d-6b67-4cec-ab64-68cdfbddebcd/preparedness-framework-v2.pdf>

name: Authorization before frontier training
short: Get a regulator's approval before you start a training run above the threshold.
trigger: Training runs above a compute threshold (10^26 FLOP or a successor).
protects: Stops a lab from building a much more powerful model until it can show it can keep it under control.
risk_why: This acts before a dangerous model exists, when prevention is easiest. It's among the stronger measures, though regulators may struggle to judge the cases.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up about 4 weeks behind where it would be; China loses about 2 days more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: Whether the regulator can say no, and how long it takes to say yes.
requires: Before beginning a training run above the threshold, submit a safety and security plan for the run and receive authorization. | The regulator may impose conditions or withhold approval. | Distinct from SB 1047, which required a self-certified protocol before training but no approval.
baseline: No U.S. law does this. SB 1047 required a written protocol and cybersecurity before training, self-certified. The EU AI Act requires notification, not approval. A true licensing gate on training has been proposed by think tanks and in early drafts of federal bills but not enacted.
reasoning:
The model distinguishes raw authorization waiting from research preserved during waiting. Only serial stages count toward frontier delay; parallel training runs increase workload. The first affected checkpoint arrives after a pipeline delay, preserving existing models and ongoing runs.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is about 4 weeks behind its baseline path and China's is about 2 days behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, about 3.5 weeks, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: Licensing regimes in other industries take far longer than 30 days once they mature, and a regulator that can say no will eventually say no. The first refusal costs a generation, not a month. A lab also cannot plan a run it does not know will be approved, so the parallel-filing assumption breaks down as the regime tightens. Three months could be the floor rather than the ceiling.

name: Thirty-day pre-training notice
short: File a plan 30 days before a frontier run. No approval needed, but the clock runs.
trigger: Training runs above a compute threshold.
protects: Gives the government a heads-up before the biggest AI models are built.
risk_why: Advance notice stops nothing by itself. It helps the government prepare and respond.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up about 3 days behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: Whether labs actually know 30 days out that a run will happen.
requires: Notify the regulator at least 30 days before starting a training run above the threshold, with a description of the run and its safety plan. | No approval is required; the run may proceed when the period ends.
baseline: The 2023 U.S. executive order on AI required reporting on large training runs but was rescinded in January 2025. The EU AI Act requires notification within two weeks of a model meeting the systemic-risk threshold, which is after the fact. No current U.S. rule imposes a pre-run waiting period.
reasoning:
The statutory notice duration is not treated as 30 lost days for every training run. Planning lead time, material changes and work conducted in parallel determine the residual. Additional qualifying runs do not automatically become serial frontier delays.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is about 3 days behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, about 3 days, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: The frontier is increasingly made by many mid-sized runs, not one giant run per year. If the threshold catches routine runs, a 30-day notice on each is a standing tax on iteration speed. Labs would either batch experiments, which slows learning, or design around the threshold, which slows scale.

name: Six-month training pause
short: The 2023 letter. No training of systems more powerful than the frontier for six months.
trigger: Training of systems more powerful than the current frontier.
protects: Buys six months for safety research to catch up with AI capabilities.
risk_why: Six months helps only if safety research uses the time well. Labs partly catch up afterward and China keeps going, so the lasting effect is small. A rush after the pause could even add risk.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up about 1.5 months behind where it would be; China loses about 7 days more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: Whether it ends when it says it ends.
requires: All AI labs immediately pause for at least six months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4 (the frontier at the time). | The pause should be public and verifiable and include all key actors. | If it cannot be enacted quickly, governments should step in and institute a moratorium.
baseline: Proposed on March 22, 2023 by the Future of Life Institute letter, which now shows more than 31,000 signatures. Not enacted anywhere. Training did not pause.
reasoning:
This is a six-month U.S.-only pause, with China continuing, as in the menu’s original pricing convention. Below-threshold research and permitted methods continue. Restarting partially recovers the scaling gap before month 12. The maximum loss during the pause differs from the endpoint loss.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is about 1.5 months behind its baseline path and China's is about 7 days behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, about 1.5 months, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: The letter asked for a pause by every key actor, including China. If that happened, the lead cost is zero by definition. It did not happen and would not. As a unilateral policy, this is the most expensive item on the menu and the steelman for a higher price is that "at least six months" has no upper bound.
sources: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter (March 2023) <https://futureoflife.org/open-letter/pause-giant-ai-experiments/>

name: Hard cap on training compute
short: No training run above a fixed ceiling set at about today's largest runs, and the ceiling never rises.
trigger: All training runs above the cap (say 10^27 FLOP).
protects: Stops anyone in the U.S. training models much more powerful than today's.
risk_why: Capping scale directly limits how capable U.S. models get. But it doesn't bind China and pushes progress into better algorithms, so the effect is uncertain.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up about 4 months behind where it would be; China loses about 8 days more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
recurrence: Per year the cap stays in place
uncertainty: How much frontier progress comes from compute scaling versus algorithms and post-training.
requires: Prohibit training runs above a fixed compute threshold. | The threshold does not rise with time.
baseline: No jurisdiction has a hard cap. Thresholds in SB 53 and the EU AI Act trigger obligations, not prohibitions.
reasoning:
A permanent ceiling progressively binds as baseline training compute grows. Reallocation to other experiments, algorithmic work and permitted inference/post-training recover part of the lost scale. The result is an endpoint shortfall, not a fixed annual bill to add forever.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is about 4 months behind its baseline path and China's is about 8 days behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, about 4 months, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: Compute is the input the U.S. leads on. Epoch and RAND put the U.S. hardware lead at about four years and its compute capacity at roughly ten times China's. A cap surrenders the one advantage that export controls protect. The lead cost could be the entire lead within two years.

name: Safety checks before internal use
short: Test and safeguard a model before the lab's own researchers use it, not just before the public does.
trigger: Frontier models, at the point of internal deployment.
protects: Catches dangerous models before labs use them in-house, where they help build the next model.
risk_why: Many risk scenarios start inside the lab, where a powerful model helps build its successor. Checking models before internal use targets that.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up about 1 day behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: How long labs would hold a model back from their own staff while tests finish.
requires: Complete dangerous-capability evaluations before a frontier model is deployed inside the lab. | Put required safeguards in place before internal use, not only before public release. | California SB 53 already requires large developers to assess catastrophic risk from internal use and send the state summaries every three months.
baseline: Labs already test models before release, and some safeguards now apply internally. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra system card says its Preparedness Framework required safeguards even for internal deployment because of the model's cyber capabilities. California's SB 53 requires a framework for managing risk from internal use. What labs do not do is hold every new model back from their own staff until testing is done.
reasoning:
A newer model improves some research tasks over the predecessor already available. The model charges that incremental research productivity during the gate, using exposed task share and model cadence. It does not charge the same capability both as a calendar delay and as lost research output.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is about 1 day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, about 1 day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: As labs automate more of their own research, the internal window becomes the whole race. If a model has to wait for full testing before it can help build its successor, and testing keeps getting longer, the cost could reach a month or more per generation and compound.

name: Human sign-off on automated AI research
short: AI agents can assist with AI research, but humans must direct and approve it.
trigger: Frontier developers using AI systems to automate their own research.
protects: Keeps humans in charge as AI starts doing AI research, which could otherwise speed up beyond anyone's oversight.
risk_why: Many researchers see AI automating AI research as the step where progress could outrun oversight. Keeping humans in the loop targets that directly.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up about 4 days behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: How much faster AI-run research is making the labs, which they are only starting to measure.
requires: Require a human to direct and approve research experiments carried out by AI agents inside frontier labs. | Prohibit fully autonomous AI research loops above a capability threshold. | Report the share of research work done by AI systems.
baseline: Both major frameworks already treat automated AI research as a danger sign. Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy v3.4 has an automated R&D threshold met if its models could fully substitute for its research scientists and engineers, or if AI progress doubled in speed. OpenAI's Preparedness Framework lists fully automated AI R&D as a Critical capability. Neither framework limits today's partial automation.
reasoning:
Existing human oversight is already in the baseline. Incremental checkpoints create service and handoff delays, magnified when reviewers are busy. Only affected task chains are charged. Fully autonomous work rises under an explicit first-year scenario rather than being assumed ubiquitous today.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is about 4 days behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, about 4 days, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: This is the policy most likely to get more expensive over time. If AI research automation is the main driver of progress in 2027 and beyond, keeping humans in every loop could halve the pace of the frontier. China's labs would face no such limit.
sources: Anthropic, When AI builds itself <https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement> | OpenAI, Research acceleration: the view inside OpenAI (Sept 2026) <https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/> | Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy v3.4 <https://cdn.sanity.io/files/4zrzovbb/website/0bacdc8440ea96e62a8766d99ebe1d4eea6d5f3a.pdf> | OpenAI Preparedness Framework v2 <https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/18a02b5d-6b67-4cec-ab64-68cdfbddebcd/preparedness-framework-v2.pdf>

name: One-third of AI research budgets on safety
short: At least a third of AI R&D spending goes to safety, as leading researchers proposed in Science.
trigger: Frontier developers' AI research budgets, including compute.
protects: Makes labs spend far more on learning to control AI, not just on making it stronger.
risk_why: Safety gets a small share of lab research today. Moving to a third speeds up the work that every other safeguard depends on.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up about 1 months behind where it would be; China loses about 3 days more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: How much labs already spend on safety, which none of them publish.
requires: Allocate at least one-third of AI research and development budgets to safety and ethical use. | Count compute, not just salaries.
baseline: Labs spend real money on safety research and testing but do not publish the share. Estimates in public discussion range from a few percent to perhaps a tenth of compute at the most safety-focused labs.
reasoning:
The one-third requirement covers R&D budgets. A one-week AI-R&D compute snapshot at one lab is informative but is not a measurement of industry-wide total-budget safety shares. Safety-capability overlap and a possible budget response reduce displacement. A permanent share change is a level/resource shock, not another identical annual delay.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is about 1 months behind its baseline path and China's is about 3 days behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, about 1 months, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: If labs spend far less than a tenth on safety today, the rule could take a quarter or more of their compute, and the cost would approach two months a year. Safety research also competes for the same scarce senior researchers.
sources: Bengio, Hinton et al., Managing extreme AI risks amid rapid progress, Science (May 2024) <https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.17688> | Epoch AI, Training compute of frontier AI models grows by 4-5x per year <https://epoch.ai/blog/training-compute-of-frontier-ai-models-grows-by-4-5x-per-year> | Epoch AI, Algorithmic progress in language models <https://epoch.ai/blog/algorithmic-progress-in-language-models>

name: Product liability for AI harms
short: Victims can sue AI companies when their systems cause harm, under federal product liability law.
trigger: Developers and deployers of AI systems.
protects: Makes labs pay for serious harms their models cause, so they have a reason to prevent them.
risk_why: Paying for harms gives labs a reason to be careful. But no company can pay for a true catastrophe, so the incentive is weakest where it matters most.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: How much caution the threat of lawsuits actually buys, and whether it spills over from product decisions into research.
requires: Classify AI systems as products for liability purposes. | Create a federal cause of action for product liability claims when an AI system causes harm (the AI LEAD Act, S. 2937).
baseline: AI companies already face ordinary lawsuits, and many are pending. What they do not face is a clear federal rule that treats AI systems as products, which would make those suits easier to bring and win.
reasoning:
The financing channel multiplies exposed investment, an added risk premium, an investment response and productive redirection. A separate trust/demand offset allows net gains. Recent economics informs the channels; no medical-device coefficient is mechanically transplanted into frontier AI.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: Open-ended liability can freeze a whole field. If juries treat any misuse of a general-purpose model as a product defect, labs could slow every release, stop publishing open models, and move research abroad. That could cost months, not weeks.
sources: Durbin, Hawley introduce bill allowing victims to sue AI companies (Sept 29, 2025) <https://www.durbin.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/durbin-hawley-introduce-bill-allowing-victims-to-sue-ai-companies> | S. 2937 bill status (govinfo) <https://www.govinfo.gov/bulkdata/BILLSTATUS/119/s/BILLSTATUS-119s2937.xml>

name: Consent to train on copyrighted work
short: No training on copyrighted works or personal data without clear, affirmative consent.
trigger: Training of generative AI systems on copyrighted works or personal data.
protects: Protects writers, artists and other creators whose work trains AI.
risk_why: A copyright and fairness rule. It doesn't target catastrophic risk.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up about 4.5 weeks behind where it would be; China loses about 4 days more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: How much training data labs could license quickly, and how much capability depends on the rest.
requires: Obtain clear, affirmative consent before using copyrighted works or personal data, including to train a generative AI system (AI Accountability and Personal Data Protection Act, S. 2367). | Give individuals a right to sue for use without consent.
baseline: Labs have begun licensing some data from publishers and paid to settle past claims. Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement with authors covered about 482,000 pirated books and only past conduct. Most training data is still used without explicit consent.
reasoning:
Quality-adjusted unique data can be licensed, replaced, repeated or traded against parameters. The model reoptimizes the training recipe. Published saturation coefficients come from smaller models, so frontier transport and legally available substitutions remain important assumptions.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is about 4.5 weeks behind its baseline path and China's is about 4 days behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, about 4 weeks, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: Chinese labs would not follow U.S. consent rules. If the rule removes a large share of high-quality text and code, the capability hit could persist for years, not a single training run.

Anthropic settlement gets preliminary approval <https://www.authorsalliance.org/2025/09/28/bartz-v-anthropic-settlement-gets-preliminary-approval-key-takeaways/> | Epoch AI, Will we run out of data? <https://epoch.ai/blog/will-we-run-out-of-data-limits-of-llm-scaling-based-on-human-generated-data>

name: Background checks for lab staff
short: A standard background check for all lab employees, with no clearance-level vetting.
trigger: All employees of frontier developers.
protects: Makes it harder for spies or bad actors to get jobs inside frontier labs.
risk_why: Background checks make insider threats slightly harder but won't stop a determined state spy.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China falls under a day directly. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: How much insider risk standard checks remove, which nobody has measured.
requires: Background checks for all employees (RAND security level 3). | Risk-based screening scaled to access, rather than blanket exclusion (as proposed in Just Security, 2026).
baseline: Many labs already run some background screening. None publish how thorough it is.
reasoning:
This is ordinary background screening with work continuing where possible. It does not assume citizenship exclusion. Both the affected insider risk and productive days blocked are marginal to checks already conducted.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is under a day behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, under a day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: Even light checks can deter strong candidates who value privacy, and they can be applied unevenly to foreign-born researchers. If that pushes a few key people to labs abroad, the cost is larger than a few days.
sources: RAND, Securing AI Model Weights (2024) <https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html> | Just Security, Vetting foreign AI talent: security without exclusion (2026) <https://www.justsecurity.org/145569/vetting-foreign-ai-talent-security-without-exclusion/>

name: Clearance-level vetting for lab staff
short: Background checks for all staff; clearance-level vetting for anyone who touches the model weights.
trigger: Frontier developers' staff with access to model weights or key research.
protects: Screens staff with access to the most powerful models the way governments screen people with access to secrets.
risk_why: Clearance-level vetting is what governments use for secrets. It makes insider theft much harder.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up about 2 days behind where it would be; China falls under a day directly; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: How many researchers vetting would slow down or exclude, and how much espionage it would actually stop.
requires: Background checks for all employees (RAND security level 3). | A personnel reliability program for staff with direct access to model weights (RAND security level 4).
baseline: Labs run some insider-threat programs, but none require government-style clearances. No 2025 or 2026 bill would mandate them. The Advanced AI Security Readiness Act asks the NSA to consider personnel vetting, and Senator Banks asked nine AI CEOs about their vetting in April 2026.
reasoning:
Sensitive roles, interim access, hiring flow, productive work retained during waiting and departures are modeled separately. A portion of lost U.S. capacity may join Chinese research. Government clearance processing time is a context anchor, not an observed private-lab delay.
In the model, a year after the rule takes effect, U.S. capability is about 2 days behind its baseline path and China's is under a day behind at the model's central assumption about dependence. The difference, about 1 day, is the model's central estimate. The full calculation, every input and its evidence status are on this rule's page in the technical appendix.
steelman: If vetting drove even a tenth of top researchers out of U.S. labs, many would go to labs elsewhere, some in China. That could cost months, and it would hand talent to the country the rule is meant to protect against.

name: Ban on superintelligence
short: Ban AI that outperforms people across most areas, and pause advanced development until regulators set rules.
trigger: Frontier AI development above compute thresholds set each year.
protects: Stops U.S. labs from building AI smarter than humans until there's a way to control it.
risk_why: It directly stops U.S. labs from building the systems people worry about most. China isn't bound, and a ban is hard to define and enforce, so the range is very wide.
how: A pause with no end date, measured a year in: training stops while research continues, with no catch-up because the pause doesn't end. We estimate about 5.5 months behind, on the same logic as the modeled six-month pause.
uncertainty: How long the pause would last and how much research would continue during it.
requires: Permanently prohibit superintelligent AI, defined as exceeding humans across most domains or able to disempower humanity. | Pause advanced AI development until a new cabinet-level Department of AI sets safety rules. | Use compute thresholds, updated yearly, to target recursive self-improvement; penalties up to 20 years in prison. | Direct the U.S. to seek international agreements.
baseline: No lab has stopped frontier development. Polls show broad public support for going slower: a 2025 Future of Life Institute poll found 64% of Americans say superhuman AI should not be built until proven safe, or never.
reasoning:
Senators Sanders and Representative Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act on September 23, 2026. It pairs a permanent ban on superintelligence with a pause on advanced development until a new Department of AI writes rules, which could take a year or more.
While the pause holds, large training runs stop. Research on existing models continues, and hardware and recipes keep improving, but with no end date there is no catch-up within the year. On the simulation model's logic for the six-month pause, we estimate the U.S. frontier ends the year about 5.5 months behind where it would have been, with a range of about 3.5 to 8 months.
steelman: A pause with no end date may last far longer than a year, and a permanent ban on the most capable systems would end the U.S. frontier altogether. If China does not join, the lead would be gone within the first year.
sources: Sanders and Casar introduce the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sept 23, 2026) <https://www.sanders.senate.gov/press-releases/news-sanders-casar-introduce-legislation-to-create-new-federal-agency-to-ban-artificial-superintelligence-pause-advanced-ai-development/> | NBC News on the Sanders–Casar bill (Sept 23, 2026) <https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/bernie-sanders-greg-casar-propose-ai-superintelligence-ban-20-year-jai-rcna599460> | Statement on Superintelligence (Oct 2025) <https://superintelligence-statement.org/> | Future of Life Institute poll on superhuman AI (2025) <https://futureoflife.org/recent-news/americans-want-regulation-or-prohibition-of-superhuman-ai/>

name: Verified six-month pause with China
short: Both countries pause frontier training for six months, with verification.
trigger: Frontier training runs in both the U.S. and China.
protects: Stops both America and China from racing ahead while safety catches up.
risk_why: Both sides stopping removes the race pressure behind risky shortcuts. It's temporary and hard to verify, so the lasting effect is moderate.
how: Both countries pause six months. America loses about 51 days, as in the modeled six-month pause. We assume imperfect verification lets China keep about a fifth of its progress, so China loses about 40 days. Net: about 11 days.
uncertainty: Whether a pause can be verified. The key technologies have not been built or tested.
requires: Both countries halt training runs above an agreed threshold for six months. | Verify compliance through chip tracking, monitored data centers and inspections.
baseline: There is no U.S.–China agreement on frontier AI. In November 2024 Biden and Xi affirmed human control over nuclear launch decisions. In September 2026 the U.S. proposed an AI dialogue with a mechanism for notifying each other of serious incidents.
reasoning:
Every other pause on the menu assumes the U.S. acts alone. A verified mutual pause is what the 2023 open letter actually asked for, and it changes the math: if both sides stop, the gap does not move.
The catch is verification. Researchers writing on verification in 2025 found that many of the needed technologies have yet to be built or stress-tested. The simulation model prices a six-month U.S. pause at about 51 days behind a year later. We assume imperfect verification lets China keep about a fifth of that, so China loses about 40 days and the net is about 11 days. With good verification it could be close to zero; with poor verification it approaches the unilateral price.
steelman: A verification regime would take years to build, so a pause agreed quickly would rely on trust. If China kept most of its progress, the U.S. would lose close to the full six months.

name: Limits on releasing open-weight models
short: No publishing the weights of models above a capability threshold. API access stays allowed.
trigger: Models above a capability threshold.
protects: Keeps the most dangerous models from being downloaded by anyone, including terrorists and rival states.
risk_why: Once weights are public, safeguards can be stripped out. But open models also help safety research, and Chinese labs already release large open models, so this is debated.
how: Our estimate on the model's logic: under a day for the U.S. open ecosystem, since U.S. frontier labs are mostly closed. China loses about a day through its dependence on U.S. models at "a little."
uncertainty: How much China gains from U.S. open weights when Chinese labs already publish the largest open models.
requires: Prohibit publishing the weights of models above a capability threshold. | Allow access through hosted APIs and apps.
baseline: No U.S. law restricts open weights. The 2025 AI Action Plan encourages open models and leaves the release decision to developers. Most U.S. frontier models are closed; Chinese labs release the largest open models.
reasoning:
NTIA's 2024 report found current evidence insufficient to justify restrictions and recommended monitoring. The 2025 AI Action Plan backs open models. In 2026, after Chinese labs released near-frontier open models, officials floated restrictions on Chinese open models; Anthropic said it has never advocated a ban.
Hugging Face reports that in almost every month of 2026, the largest open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any American one. That limits how much China gains from U.S. open weights. U.S. frontier labs mostly keep their best weights closed already, so we estimate under a day of lost U.S. progress. Denied open weights slow China by about a day at the "a little" setting, more if China depends heavily on U.S. models.
steelman: Open models are how most researchers, universities and startups work with frontier AI. Closing them could slow U.S. research broadly and cede the open ecosystem to Chinese models, which already lead downloads.

name: Sell advanced AI chips to China
short: License sales of advanced chips like Nvidia's H200 to China.
trigger: Exports of advanced AI chips to China.
protects: Not a safety rule. It lets U.S. chipmakers sell advanced chips to China.
risk_why: It speeds China's labs. The effect on risk is debated.
how: Our estimate on the model's export-control logic, which prices relaxing all controls at about four weeks: licensing H200-class chips alone is about two weeks, with deliveries so far far below the cap.
uncertainty: How many chips China actually buys. Deliveries so far are a small fraction of what is licensed.
requires: License exports of H200-class chips to approved Chinese buyers, case by case. | Cap China's shipments at 50% of U.S. shipments of the same chip; require U.S. testing and buyer security procedures. | Government takes a share of revenue.
baseline: In January 2026 the Commerce Department moved H200 licenses to case-by-case review with a 50% cap. China's government initially blocked purchases; by August 2026, ByteDance and Tencent had each received about 10,000 H200s.
reasoning:
The Institute for Progress estimates the U.S. lead in AI compute produced in 2026 is 21 to 49 times with no exports, falling to between 6.7 and 1.2 times with unrestricted H200 sales. IAPS estimates the licensed cap would raise China's total 2026 processing power by more than 250%, and CNAS estimates the cap allows about 890,000 H200s.
Converting compute to progress: a 3.5-fold increase in compute is roughly nine months of compute growth at fivefold a year, and compute drives most progress. At full use of the cap that would be several months of lead a year. The simulation model finds that relaxing all chip controls now would cost about four weeks of lead a year in, because compute takes time to turn into better models. Licensing H200-class chips alone, with deliveries so far far below the cap, we price at about two weeks, with a range of a few days to about six weeks.
steelman: If China buys up to the cap, the compute gap could shrink from dozens of times to nearly even within a year, and the lead would erode faster than any safety rule on the menu could cost.

name: Location verification for AI chips
short: Require exported AI chips to verify their location, to stop smuggling to China.
trigger: Export-controlled AI chips and their exporters.
protects: Stops advanced chips from being smuggled to China.
risk_why: It makes smuggling harder. The effect on risk is debated.
how: Our estimate on the model's export-control logic: cutting smuggling, which may supply about a third of China's compute, is worth about 5 days a year in.
uncertainty: How much smuggling verification would stop, and how quickly smugglers would adapt.
requires: Within 180 days, require location verification on export-controlled AI chips (Chip Security Act). | Require exporters to report diversion or tampering. | Study further security mechanisms within a year.
baseline: Not yet law. The Chip Security Act passed a House committee in March 2026 and was added to the Senate's defense bill in July 2026. Nvidia has released opt-in location tools.
reasoning:
CNAS estimated that 10,000 to several hundred thousand chips were smuggled to China in 2024. Epoch AI's 2026 analysis puts the total through 2025 at a median of 660,000 H100-equivalents, about a third of China's compute. The Justice Department indicted three people in March 2026 over about $2.5 billion of allegedly diverted servers.
If location verification cut smuggling by a third to a half, China would lose roughly a sixth of its compute. At fivefold yearly compute growth that is about a month of compute progress, and compute drives most progress, but the simulation model shows compute changes take time to show up in capability. We price about 5 days of Chinese delay a year in, with a range of zero to about two weeks.
steelman: Smugglers adapt: they rent chips abroad, route through third countries, or spoof location checks. If verification only shifts smuggling into cloud rental, the benefit could be near zero.

name: Federal preemption of state AI laws
short: One national rulebook: states may not regulate frontier AI development.
trigger: State laws that regulate AI developers.
protects: Replaces state AI laws with one federal standard. It removes protections rather than adding them.
risk_why: It removes the state frontier laws, which together cut about 3% of the risk here. A federal replacement could add some of that back.
how: Our estimate: removes the state frontier laws, which the model prices at under a day combined.
uncertainty: How much the broader patchwork of state AI laws, beyond frontier laws, actually slows frontier labs. No study has measured it.
requires: Prohibit states from adopting or enforcing laws that impose new obligations on AI developers. | Leave generally applicable laws and protections for minors in place, as most proposals do.
baseline: No preemption law has passed. The Senate stripped a 10-year moratorium 99–1 in July 2025. An executive order in December 2025 created a Justice Department task force to challenge state laws; it had filed no lawsuits by September 2026. A House draft would preempt state laws on development for three years.
reasoning:
The frontier-specific state laws on this menu, California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act, each cost under a day in the simulation model, and they largely overlap. Preempting them buys back under a day.
The broader patchwork is larger. Thirty-eight states adopted around 100 AI measures in 2025, according to NCSL. But most regulate how AI is used by deployers, in hiring, insurance or chatbots, and rarely touch how frontier labs train models. We found no study measuring their effect on frontier progress. We price the frontier effect at under a day, with a range up to half a day.
steelman: Supporters argue the real cost of a patchwork is not paperwork but uncertainty: fifty different liability rules could make labs slower and more cautious across every product. If that is right, preemption is worth more than a week.

name: $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas

trigger: New H-1B petitions.
protects: Not a safety rule. It changes who can come to America to work on AI.
risk_why: It changes the pace of U.S. progress, not safety practices. No clear effect on risk.
how: Our estimate: about 2 days a year in, mostly from a thinner pipeline of students and researchers. Labs can pay the fee.
uncertainty: How much a fee changes who comes to the U.S. to study and work in AI. The fee is currently blocked in court.
requires: Pay $100,000 with each new H-1B petition (2025 proclamation); renewals exempt. | A proposed 2026 regulation would set a $103,265 fee on cap-subject petitions, exempting universities and nonprofit research groups.
baseline: The fee took effect in September 2025, was vacated by a federal court in June 2026, and remains unenforceable. The proclamation was extended to September 2027. New international student enrollment fell 17% in fall 2025.
reasoning:
CSET found in 2019 that two-thirds of graduate students in AI-related programs were international and that most stay in the U.S. after graduating. The Institute for Progress found that 25 of the 42 U.S. companies on the Forbes AI 50 had an immigrant founder, and most of those founders first came on student visas.
A $100,000 fee is small next to a frontier researcher's pay, so large labs would mostly absorb it. The effect falls on startups, universities and the students who become tomorrow's researchers. The pipeline effect builds slowly, so a year in we estimate about 2 days of lost progress, with a range of under a day to about a week.
steelman: Talent compounds. If the U.S. becomes a less reliable destination, top students go elsewhere, and some go to China. The cost could grow year after year and exceed a month.

name: Fast-track visas for AI researchers
short: Faster visas and green cards for top AI researchers.
trigger: AI researchers and STEM graduates seeking U.S. visas.
protects: Not a safety rule. It brings more AI talent to America.
risk_why: It changes the pace of U.S. progress, not safety practices. No clear effect on risk.
how: Our estimate, the mirror image of the H-1B fee: about 2 days gained a year in.
uncertainty: How many additional top researchers faster visas would actually bring or keep.
requires: Exempt U.S. STEM master's and PhD graduates from green-card caps (Keep STEM Talent Act). | Expand and speed O-1A visas and recapture unused green cards (Institute for Progress proposals).

CSET found most international AI PhDs take U.S. jobs and stay at least five years, so the main effect of fast-track visas is at the margin: more arrivals, fewer departures, and less time lost to visa limbo. The Institute for Progress argues international talent is necessary for U.S. AI leadership.

name: Fast permits and power for AI data centers
short: Faster environmental reviews and grid connections for AI data centers and power plants.
trigger: Data centers over 100 megawatts and the generation that serves them.
protects: Not a safety rule. It gets AI data centers built faster.
risk_why: It speeds up U.S. progress. That may add a little risk by speeding the race, but the effect is unclear.
how: Our estimate on the model's compute logic: if faster permits bring part of new compute online a couple of months sooner, the frontier gains about 10 days a year in.
uncertainty: How much permitting, as opposed to chips, turbines and transformers, is the binding limit on new compute.
requires: Create faster environmental review paths and federal-land siting for data centers over 100 megawatts (July 2025 executive order). | Speed grid interconnection for large loads and new generation. | Pass permitting reform such as the SPEED Act.
baseline: The July 2025 order is in effect. FERC ordered grid operators in June 2026 to address large-load interconnection. The SPEED Act passed the House in December 2025; Senate talks were ongoing in September 2026.
reasoning:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory finds that the median time from an interconnection request to operation exceeded five years for projects built in 2025. Anthropic estimates U.S. AI will need at least 50 gigawatts by 2028 and contrasts China's months-long permitting with U.S. reviews that take years. The Institute for Progress says flexible connections can bring a 500 megawatt data center online three to five years sooner.
In the simulation model, compute is one input among several and labs partly substitute when it is scarce. If faster permitting brings part of new compute online a couple of months sooner, we estimate the frontier ends the year about 10 days ahead. The range runs from a day to about six weeks because other bottlenecks, like chips and transformers, may bind first.
steelman: For a lower gain: labs build where power is already available, and chips, not permits, set the pace. For a higher one: if power is the binding constraint by 2027, permitting could be worth several months a year.

name: Public AI research compute
short: Government computing power for university and public AI research.
trigger: Researchers outside frontier labs.
protects: Gives universities computing power, some of it for safety research.
risk_why: It could help academic safety research slightly.
how: Our estimate: the public resource is tiny next to frontier labs, under a day.
uncertainty: Whether public research feeds frontier progress through ideas rather than compute.
requires: Fund the National AI Research Resource permanently (CREATE AI Act). | Build California's public compute cluster, CalCompute, if funded.

CSET estimated the pilot's compute at about 3.77 exaFLOPS, roughly equal to 5,000 H100 chips, while companies like Meta and Microsoft each bought over 150,000 H100s. Public compute supports academic research and training, which matters for the long-run talent pipeline, but it does not move the frontier's own training runs.

name: A government "Manhattan Project" for AI
short: A federally funded crash program to build the most advanced AI.
trigger: Federal AI research and compute.
protects: Not a safety rule. A government push to build the most powerful AI first.
risk_why: A government race could add risk by speeding things up and sidelining safety. It could also put the most powerful AI under public control. Debated, leaning toward more risk.
how: Our estimate on the model's compute logic: a program adding roughly a tenth more compute would gain about 12 days a year in. Depends entirely on size.
uncertainty: The program's size, and whether China would respond by racing harder.
requires: Establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program to acquire advanced AI capability (USCC 2024 recommendation). | The 2025 Genesis Mission instead builds a Department of Energy AI platform for science, with about $5 billion in announced commitments.
baseline: No crash program exists. The Genesis Mission launched in November 2025 and announced over $5 billion in commitments across 278 projects in July 2026.
reasoning:
The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission's first 2024 recommendation was a Manhattan Project-like program racing to AGI. The 2025 Genesis Mission borrows the Manhattan Project comparison but funds science applications at a far smaller scale.
Private frontier spending already runs to hundreds of billions of dollars a year. A government program adds on top, and could help most by clearing power and chip bottlenecks. Using the simulation model's link between compute and progress, a program adding about a tenth more frontier compute would put the U.S. about 12 days ahead a year in. The range runs from a couple of days for a Genesis-sized program to about two months for a large crash effort. We do not model China's likely response, which could offset some of the gain.
steelman: A crash program could provoke China to race harder and abandon any safety cooperation, erasing the gain. Critics also argue it would concentrate power and sideline safety.

name: DNA synthesis screening
short: Screen synthetic DNA orders and customers to block bioweapon ingredients.
trigger: Providers of synthetic DNA and RNA.
protects: Stops someone from using AI's help to order the DNA for a bioweapon.
risk_why: Biological weapons are one of the most cited ways AI could help cause mass casualties. Screening DNA orders blocks a key physical step.
how: No cost to AI developers: the burden falls on DNA synthesis providers.
uncertainty: None for the lead. Whether screening works against AI-designed sequences is a separate question.
requires: Require DNA synthesis providers to screen orders against sequences of concern and verify customers (Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act, S.3741). | Require federally funded institutions to buy only from screening providers (2024 framework; AI Action Plan).
baseline: A 2024 framework made screening a condition of federal research funding; a 2025 executive order called for it to be revised or replaced. A Cotton–Klobuchar bill introduced in January 2026 is in committee.
reasoning:
This is a safety rule that never touches an AI lab. The cost falls on DNA synthesis providers, several of which, like Twist and IDT, endorse the Cotton–Klobuchar bill. It addresses the risk that AI lowers the barrier to building biological weapons, which a 2025 Science paper illustrated by showing AI-redesigned toxins slipping past screening software.
