name: Watermarks on AI-generated content
short: Hidden labels on AI-generated images, video and audio, plus a free detection tool.
trigger: Generative AI providers with large user bases; in the EU, all general-purpose model providers.
protects: Helps people tell real photos, video and audio from AI fakes.
risk_why: It targets fraud and misinformation, not catastrophic risk.
how: Our estimate: engineering work to label outputs displaces under a day of research.
uncertainty: How much engineering reliable watermarking takes, especially for text in the EU.
requires: Embed hidden, machine-readable provenance in AI-generated image, video and audio (California AI Transparency Act, operative August 2, 2026). | Offer a visible label and a free public detection tool. | EU AI Act Article 50: mark AI outputs in a machine-readable format.

California's AI Transparency Act became operative on August 2, 2026, and the EU's transparency rules applied from the same date, with a grace period to December 2026 for existing systems. Both lean on standards like C2PA that the largest labs helped build.

name: Safety rules for AI companion chatbots
short: AI disclosure, crisis protocols and protections for minors in companion chatbots.
trigger: Operators of companion chatbots; possibly general-purpose assistants.
protects: Protects kids and vulnerable people from harmful chatbot conversations.
risk_why: It targets harm to individual users, not catastrophic risk.
how: Our estimate: product safeguards displace under a day of research.
uncertainty: Whether general-purpose assistants like ChatGPT and Claude count as companion chatbots, and how heavy age verification would be under the GUARD Act.
requires: Disclose that the chatbot is an AI; maintain a suicide and self-harm protocol with crisis referrals (California SB 243, effective January 1, 2026). | For known minors: break reminders every three hours and no sexual content. | Annual risk assessments and audits for child safety (California SB 1119, effective July 2027).

The Future of Privacy Forum notes uncertainty about whether general-purpose assistants are covered; OpenAI's support for California's 2026 law suggests it expects to be.

name: Rules against algorithmic discrimination
short: Documentation, notice and appeals when AI makes consequential decisions about people.
trigger: AI used in consequential decisions such as jobs, lending and housing.
protects: Protects people from unfair AI decisions about jobs, loans and housing.
risk_why: It targets unfair decisions about individuals, not catastrophic risk.
how: Our estimate: documentation work displaces under a day of research.
uncertainty: Whether other states adopt heavier duties of care than Colorado's current documentation rule.
requires: Developers give deployers documentation on intended uses, training-data categories and known limitations, and keep records for three years (Colorado SB26-189, effective January 1, 2027). | Deployers give notice, explain adverse decisions within 30 days and offer human review.

protects: Makes insurers, who would pay for disasters, check that labs are careful.

how: Our estimate on the model's logic, like product liability: underwriting and insurer audits take senior time but don't stop training. Under a day.
uncertainty: Whether insurers would offer coverage at all. Many are currently excluding AI risks from their policies.
requires: Carry liability insurance covering the insurable layer of harms from frontier systems. | Insurers, rather than developers, select third-party auditors.

name: Human control of nuclear launch decisions
short: Only humans may decide to launch nuclear weapons.
trigger: U.S. nuclear command and control.
protects: Keeps AI from ever deciding on its own to launch nuclear weapons.
risk_why: It keeps a human decision on nuclear launch. That addresses a narrow but severe risk.
how: No cost to AI developers.
uncertainty: None for the lead.
requires: Require positive human action in executing presidential decisions on nuclear weapons (FY2025 NDAA, section 1638, as a statement of policy). | Affirm human control over nuclear use decisions internationally (2024 Biden–Xi statement).

trigger: Frontier developers holding unreleased model weights.
protects: Stops hackers and foreign spies from stealing the most powerful models.
risk_why: Whoever steals a model's weights can strip out its safeguards. Strong security keeps dangerous models out of the wrong hands.
how: Simulation model, 12 months after the rule takes effect: U.S. progress ends up under a day behind where it would be; China falls under a day directly; China loses under a day more through its dependence on U.S. models, at the "a little" setting. Most of the model's inputs are stated assumptions.
uncertainty: The probability that frontier weights get stolen in a given year, which nobody outside the labs and intelligence agencies can estimate.

reasoning:
An SL3-like floor is incremental to existing voluntary hardening. Hazard reduction, current asset value, assimilation and decay determine the benefit. Research effort and ongoing friction determine the U.S. cost. The compromise rate and effectiveness are explicit priors.

name: Isolated secure development environment

protects: Cuts lab systems off from the internet so models and secrets can't leak or be stolen.

If the penalty is 30% and it compounds across a field where the frontier doubles every 105 days, the U.S. hands away a third of its own progress to protect against a threat it cannot quantify. trigger: Compute providers serving customers at frontier scale.
protects: Stops bad actors and banned foreign labs from secretly renting U.S. computing power.

uncertainty: How much Chinese frontier training currently runs on rented Western compute.

protects: Stops rivals from copying U.S. models by training on their answers.

trigger: Exports of advanced AI chips and manufacturing equipment to China.
protects: Keeps China's military and labs from getting the best U.S. chips.

protects: Stops every country, China included, from building AI smarter than humans until it can be done safely.
